dashboard.predictionInfoDetail: Predictions are based on {{name}}'s recent sleep patterns. You can adjust the number of naps in Settings.
dashboard.predictionInfoDetailGeneric: Predictions are based on recent sleep patterns. You can adjust the number of naps in Settings.
dashboard.infoSettingsBody: We use your baby's sleep patterns to predict nap times and the number of naps per day. The more you track, the more accurate predictions become. If you'd prefer to set wake windows manually, you can do so in Sleep Settings.
dashboard.infoMissedNapBody: Even with good predictions, sometimes babies just aren't ready to sleep. Sleep is influenced by routine, environment, and your child's development. If your little one didn't fall asleep, that's okay — here's when to try again:
dashboard.infoMissedNapRetry:
2–3 months: wait ~30 min and try again
4–5 months: wait ~45 min and try again
6+ months: wait ~60 min and try again
dashboard.infoHowLongRetry:
2–3 months: try for about 30 min
4–5 months: try for about 45 min
6+ months: try for about 60 min
dashboard.infoEncouragement: Missing a nap doesn't mean you've failed. Some days just go sideways — and that's normal. You and your baby are learning together.

milestones.infoReassurance: Children develop at their own pace. These milestones show what most children (75%) can do by a certain age. If you have concerns, talk to your child's doctor — early support makes a difference.

items.2m-social-1: Calms down when spoken to or picked up
items.2m-social-3: Seems happy to see you when you walk up to her
items.2m-social-4: Smiles when you talk to or smile at her
items.2m-cognitive-2: Looks at a toy for several seconds
items.2m-movement-1: Holds head up when on tummy
items.2m-movement-2: Moves both arms and both legs
items.4m-social-1: Smiles on his own to get your attention
items.4m-social-2: Chuckles (not yet a full laugh) when you try to make him laugh
items.4m-social-3: Looks at you, moves, or makes sounds to get or keep your attention
items.4m-language-2: Makes sounds back when you talk to him
items.4m-language-3: Turns head towards the sound of your voice
items.4m-cognitive-1: If hungry, opens mouth when she sees breast or bottle
items.4m-cognitive-2: Looks at her hands with interest
items.4m-movement-1: Holds head steady without support when you are holding her
items.4m-movement-2: Holds a toy when you put it in her hand
items.4m-movement-3: Uses her arm to swing at toys
items.4m-movement-5: Pushes up onto elbows/forearms when on tummy
items.6m-social-2: Likes to look at himself in a mirror
items.6m-language-1: Takes turns making sounds with you
items.6m-cognitive-1: Puts things in her mouth to explore them
items.6m-cognitive-2: Reaches to grab a toy she wants
items.6m-cognitive-3: Closes lips to show she doesn't want more food
items.6m-movement-2: Pushes up with straight arms when on tummy
items.6m-movement-3: Leans on hands to support himself when sitting
items.9m-social-1: Is shy, clingy, or fearful around strangers
items.9m-social-2: Shows several facial expressions, like happy, sad, angry, and surprised
items.9m-social-3: Looks when you call her name
items.9m-social-4: Reacts when you leave (looks, reaches for you, or cries)
items.9m-social-5: Smiles or laughs when you play peek-a-boo
items.9m-language-2: Lifts arms up to be picked up
items.9m-cognitive-1: Looks for objects when dropped out of sight (like his spoon or toy)
items.9m-movement-1: Gets to a sitting position by herself
items.9m-movement-2: Moves things from one hand to her other hand
items.9m-movement-3: Uses fingers to "rake" food towards himself
items.1y-social-1: Plays games with you, like pat-a-cake
items.1y-social-3: Calls a parent "mama" or "dada" or another special name
items.1y-social-4: Understands "no" (pauses briefly or stops when you say it)
items.1y-language-1: Puts something in a container, like a block in a cup
items.1y-language-2: Looks for things he sees you hide, like a toy under a blanket
items.1y-movement-1: Drinks from a cup without a lid, as you hold it
items.1y-movement-2: Picks things up between thumb and pointer finger, like small bits of food
items.15m-social-1: Copies other children while playing, like taking toys out of a container when another child does
items.15m-social-2: Shows you an object she likes
items.15m-social-4: Hugs stuffed doll or other toy
items.15m-social-5: Shows you affection (hugs, cuddles, or kisses you)
items.15m-language-1: Tries to say one or two words besides "mama" or "dada", like "ba" for ball or "da" for dog
items.15m-language-2: Looks at a familiar object when you name it
items.15m-language-3: Follows directions given with both a gesture and words, e.g. he gives you a toy when you hold out your hand and say "Give me the toy"
items.15m-language-4: Points to ask for something or to get help
items.15m-cognitive-1: Tries to use things the right way, like a phone, cup, or book
items.15m-cognitive-2: Stacks at least two small objects, like blocks
items.15m-movement-1: Takes a few steps on his own
items.15m-movement-2: Uses fingers to feed herself some food
items.18m-social-1: Moves away from you, but looks to make sure you are close by
items.18m-social-2: Points to show you something interesting
items.18m-social-3: Puts hands out for you to wash them
items.18m-social-4: Looks at a few pages in a book with you
items.18m-social-5: Helps you dress him by pushing arm through sleeve or lifting up foot
items.18m-language-1: Tries to say three or more words besides "mama" or "dada"
items.18m-language-2: Follows one-step directions without any gestures, like giving you the toy when you say "Give it to me"
items.18m-cognitive-1: Copies you doing chores, like sweeping with a broom
items.18m-cognitive-2: Plays with toys in a simple way, like pushing a toy car
items.18m-movement-1: Walks without holding on to anyone or anything
items.18m-movement-3: Drinks from a cup without a lid and may spill sometimes
items.18m-movement-6: Climbs on and off a couch or chair without help
items.2y-social-1: Notices when others are hurt or upset, like pausing or looking sad when he hears someone crying
items.2y-social-2: Looks at your face to see how to react in a new situation
items.2y-language-1: Points to things in a book when you ask, like "Where is the bear?"
items.2y-language-2: Says at least two words together, like "More milk"
items.2y-language-3: Points to at least two body parts when you ask him to show you
items.2y-language-4: Uses more gestures than just waving and pointing, like blowing a kiss or nodding yes
items.2y-cognitive-1: Holds something in one hand while using the other hand, like holding a container and taking the lid off
items.2y-cognitive-2: Tries to use switches, knobs, or buttons on a toy
items.2y-cognitive-3: Plays with more than one toy at the same time, like putting toy food on a toy plate
items.2y-movement-3: Walks (not climbs) up a few stairs with or without help
items.30m-social-1: Plays next to other children and sometimes plays with them
items.30m-social-2: Shows you what she can do by saying "Look at me!"
items.30m-social-3: Follows simple routines when told, like helping to pick up toys when you say "It's clean-up time"
items.30m-language-2: Says two or more words together, with one action word, like "Doggie run"
items.30m-language-3: Names things in a book when you point and ask "What is this?"
items.30m-cognitive-1: Uses things to pretend, like feeding a block to a doll as if it were food
items.30m-cognitive-2: Shows simple problem-solving skills, like standing on a small stool to reach something
items.30m-cognitive-3: Follows two-step instructions like "Put the toy down and close the door"
items.30m-cognitive-4: Shows he knows at least one color, like pointing to a red crayon when you ask "Which one is red?"
items.30m-movement-1: Uses hands to twist things, like turning doorknobs or unscrewing lids
items.30m-movement-2: Takes some clothes off by herself, like loose pants or an open jacket
items.30m-movement-3: Jumps off the ground with both feet
items.30m-movement-4: Turns book pages, one at a time, when you read to her
items.3y-social-1: Calms down within 10 minutes after you leave her, like at a childcare drop-off
items.3y-social-2: Notices other children and joins them to play
items.3y-language-1: Talks with you in conversation using at least two back-and-forth exchanges
items.3y-language-2: Asks "who", "what", "where", or "why" questions, like "Where is mommy/daddy?"
items.3y-language-3: Says what action is happening in a picture or book when asked, like "running", "eating", or "playing"
items.3y-language-5: Talks well enough for others to understand, most of the time
items.3y-cognitive-1: Draws a circle, when you show him how
items.3y-cognitive-2: Avoids touching hot objects, like a stove, when you warn her
items.3y-movement-1: Strings items together, like large beads or macaroni
items.3y-movement-2: Puts on some clothes by himself, like loose pants or a jacket
items.4y-social-1: Pretends to be something else during play (teacher, superhero, dog)
items.4y-social-2: Asks to go play with children if none are around, like "Can I play with Alex?"
items.4y-social-3: Comforts others who are hurt or sad, like hugging a crying friend
items.4y-social-4: Avoids danger, like not jumping from tall heights at the playground
items.4y-social-6: Changes behavior based on where she is (place of worship, library, playground)
items.4y-language-1: Says sentences with four or more words
items.4y-language-2: Says some words from a song, story, or nursery rhyme
items.4y-language-3: Talks about at least one thing that happened during the day, like "I played soccer"
items.4y-language-4: Answers simple questions like "What is a coat for?" or "What is a crayon for?"
items.4y-cognitive-1: Names a few colors of items
items.4y-cognitive-2: Tells what comes next in a well-known story
items.4y-cognitive-3: Draws a person with three or more body parts
items.4y-movement-1: Catches a large ball most of the time
items.4y-movement-2: Serves himself food or pours water, with adult supervision
items.4y-movement-4: Holds crayon or pencil between fingers and thumb (not a fist)
items.5y-social-1: Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children
items.5y-social-2: Sings, dances, or acts for you
items.5y-social-3: Does simple chores at home, like matching socks or clearing the table after eating
items.5y-language-1: Tells a story she heard or made up with at least two events, like a cat was stuck in a tree and a firefighter saved it
items.5y-language-2: Answers simple questions about a book or story after you read or tell it to him
items.5y-language-3: Keeps a conversation going with more than three back-and-forth exchanges
items.5y-language-4: Uses or recognizes simple rhymes (bat-cat, ball-tall)
items.5y-cognitive-2: Names some numbers between 1 and 5 when you point to them
items.5y-cognitive-3: Uses words about time, like "yesterday", "tomorrow", "morning", or "night"
items.5y-cognitive-4: Pays attention for 5 to 10 minutes during activities, like during story time or making arts and crafts
items.5y-cognitive-5: Writes some letters in her name
items.5y-cognitive-6: Names some letters when you point to them

achievements.periodNote: You've tracked all developmental milestones for this period. Every baby develops at their own pace — this is a wonderful checkpoint.

6h.under3m: A wonderful early sign! Your baby's brain is beginning to develop its own internal clock, with melatonin production just starting to kick in.
6h.3to4m: A lovely milestone. Your baby's brain is now producing melatonin and building a day-night rhythm, helping them consolidate sleep into longer stretches.
6h.5to6m: Your baby's sleep cycles are maturing beautifully. Their brain is getting better at linking sleep cycles together, with deeper stages of sleep becoming more prominent.
6h.7plus: Your little one's circadian rhythm is well established and their sleep architecture is becoming more mature, with longer periods of deep, restorative sleep.

8h.under3m: Quite remarkable at this age! Your baby's nervous system is maturing early, already learning to transition smoothly between sleep cycles without fully waking.
8h.3to4m: A wonderful sign of neurological growth. Your baby's brain is developing the ability to transition between sleep cycles on its own — a skill that takes real developmental maturity.
8h.5to6m: Your baby's sleep is really coming together. Deeper sleep stages are now more prominent, and their brain is learning to self-soothe through natural arousals between sleep cycles.
8h.7plus: A beautiful reflection of how much your baby has grown. Their sleep architecture has matured significantly, with longer stretches of deep, restorative sleep carrying them through the night.

10h.under3m: What an extraordinary sleeper! Your baby's nervous system is showing early maturity in regulating sleep-wake patterns. Their internal clock is off to an impressive start.
10h.3to4m: A big milestone! Your baby's circadian rhythm and sleep drive are working together remarkably well, allowing deep, consolidated sleep for an extended stretch.
10h.5to6m: Your baby's sleep system is really flourishing. Their brain has made wonderful progress in linking sleep cycles, producing melatonin at the right times, and settling back to sleep naturally.
10h.7plus: A testament to your baby's growing brain. Their circadian rhythm is robust, their sleep cycles are maturing toward adult-like patterns, and their natural self-soothing ability has developed beautifully.
